<p class="center">"A knot!" said Alice. "Oh, do let me help to undo it!"</p>
<h3>ANSWERS TO KNOT I.</h3>
<p><i>Problem.</i>—"Two travellers spend from 3 o'clock till 9 in walking along
a level road, up a hill, and home again: their pace on the level being 4
miles an hour, up hill 3, and down hill 6. Find distance walked: also
(within half an hour) time of reaching top of hill."</p>
<p><i>Answer.</i>—"24 miles: half-past 6."</p>
<hr style="width: 45%;">
<p><i>Solution.</i>—A level mile takes ¼ of an hour, up hill <sup>1</sup>⁄<sub>3</sub>,
down hill
<sup>1</sup>⁄<sub>6</sub>. Hence to go and return over the same mile, whether on the level or
on the hill-side, takes ½ an hour. Hence in 6 hours they went 12 miles
out and 12 back. If the 12 miles out had been nearly all level, they
would have taken a little over 3 hours; if nearly all up hill, a little
under 4. Hence 3½ hours must be within ½ an hour of the time taken
in reaching the peak; thus, as they started at 3, they got there within
½ an hour of ½ past 6.</p>
<p><span class="pagenum"><a id="Page_78">[78]</a></span></p><hr style="width: 45%;">
<p>Twenty-seven answers have come in. Of these, 9 are right, 16 partially
right, and 2 wrong. The 16 give the <i>distance</i> correctly, but they have
failed to grasp the fact that the top of the hill might have been
reached at <i>any</i> moment between 6 o'clock and 7.</p>
<p>The two wrong answers are from <span class="smcap">Gerty Vernon</span> and <span class="smcap">A Nihilist</span>. The former
makes the distance "23 miles," while her revolutionary companion puts it
at "27." <span class="smcap">Gerty Vernon</span> says "they had to go 4 miles along the plain, and
got to the foot of the hill at 4 o'clock." They <i>might</i> have done so, I
grant; but you have no ground for saying they <i>did</i> so. "It was 7½
miles to the top of the hill, and they reached that at ¼ before 7
o'clock." Here you go wrong in your arithmetic, and I must, however
reluctantly, bid you farewell. 7½ miles, at 3 miles an hour, would
<i>not</i> require 2¾ hours. <span class="smcap">A Nihilist</span> says "Let <i>x</i> denote the whole
number of miles; <i>y</i> the number of hours to hill-top; ∴ 3<i>y</i> =
number of miles to hill-top, and <i>x</i>-3<i>y</i> = number of miles on the other
side." You bewilder me. The other side of <i>what</i>? "Of the hill," you
say. But then, how did they get home again? However, to accommodate your
views we will build a new hostelry at the foot of the hill on the
opposite side, and also assume (what I grant you is <i>possible</i>, though
it is not <i>necessarily</i> true) that there was no level road at all. Even
then you go wrong.<span class="pagenum"><a id="Page_79">[79]</a></span></p>
<p>You say</p>
<p>
<span style="margin-left: 10.5em;">"<i>y</i> = 6 - <sup>(<i>x</i> - 3<i>y</i>)</sup>⁄<sub>6</sub>,            ..... (i);</span><br>
<br>
<span style="margin-left: 10.5em;"><sup><i>x</i></sup>⁄<sub>4½</sub> = 6                        ..... (ii)."</span><br>
</p>
<p>I grant you (i), but I deny (ii): it rests on the assumption that to go
<i>part</i> of the time at 3 miles an hour, and the rest at 6 miles an hour,
comes to the same result as going the <i>whole</i> time at 4½ miles an
hour. But this would only be true if the "<i>part</i>" were an exact <i>half</i>,
i.e., if they went up hill for 3 hours, and down hill for the other 3:
which they certainly did <i>not</i> do.</p>
<p>The sixteen, who are partially right, are <span class="smcap">Agnes Bailey</span>, <span class="smcap">F. K., Fifee</span>, G.
E. B., H. P., <span class="smcap">Kit</span>, M. E. T., <span class="smcap">Mysie</span>, <span class="smcap">A Mother's Son</span>, <span class="smcap">Nairam</span>, <span class="smcap">A
Redruthian</span>, <span class="smcap">A Socialist</span>, <span class="smcap">Spear Maiden</span>, T. B. C., <span class="smcap">Vis Inertiæ</span>, and <span class="smcap">Yak</span>. Of
these, <span class="smcap">F. K., Fifee</span>, T. B. C., and <span class="smcap">Vis Inertiæ</span> do not attempt the second
part at all. F. K. and H. P. give no working. The rest make particular
assumptions, such as that there was no level road—that there were 6
miles of level road—and so on, all leading to <i>particular</i> times being
fixed for reaching the hill-top. The most curious assumption is that of
<span class="smcap">Agnes Bailey</span>, who says "Let <i>x</i> = number of hours occupied in ascent;
then <sup><i>x</i></sup>⁄<sub>2</sub> = hours occupied in descent; and <sup>4<i>x</i></sup>⁄<sub>3</sub> = hours occupied on
the<span class="pagenum"><a id="Page_80">[80]</a></span> level." I suppose you were thinking of the relative <i>rates</i>, up
hill and on the level; which we might express by saying that, if they
went <i>x</i> miles up hill in a certain time, they would go <sup>4<i>x</i></sup>⁄<sub>3</sub> miles on
the level <i>in the same time</i>. You have, in fact, assumed that they took
<i>the same time</i> on the level that they took in ascending the hill. <span class="smcap">Fifee</span>
assumes that, when the aged knight said they had gone "four miles in the
hour" on the level, he meant that four miles was the <i>distance</i> gone,
not merely the rate. This would have been—if <span class="smcap">Fifee</span> will excuse the
slang expression—a "sell," ill-suited to the dignity of the hero.</p>
<p>And now "descend, ye classic Nine!" who have solved the whole problem,
and let me sing your praises. Your names are <span class="smcap">Blithe</span>, E. W., L. B., <span class="smcap">A
Marlborough Boy</span>, O. V. L., <span class="smcap">Putney Walker</span>, <span class="smcap">Rose</span>, <span class="smcap">Sea Breeze</span>, <span class="smcap">Simple
Susan</span>, and <span class="smcap">Money Spinner</span>. (These last two I count as one, as they send a
joint answer.) <span class="smcap">Rose</span> and <span class="smcap">Simple Susan</span> and <span class="smcap">Co</span>. do not actually state that
the hill-top was reached some time between 6 and 7, but, as they have
clearly grasped the fact that a mile, ascended and descended, took the
same time as two level miles, I mark them as "right." <span class="smcap">A Marlborough Boy</span>
and <span class="smcap">Putney Walker</span> deserve honourable mention for their algebraical
solutions being the only two who have perceived<span class="pagenum"><a id="Page_81">[81]</a></span> that the question leads
to <i>an indeterminate equation</i>. E. W. brings a charge of untruthfulness
against the aged knight—a serious charge, for he was the very pink of
chivalry! She says "According to the data given, the time at the summit
affords no clue to the total distance. It does not enable us to state
precisely to an inch how much level and how much hill there was on the
road." "Fair damsel," the aged knight replies, "—if, as I surmise, thy
initials denote Early Womanhood—bethink thee that the word 'enable' is
thine, not mine. I did but ask the time of reaching the hill-top as my
<i>condition</i> for further parley. If <i>now</i> thou wilt not grant that I am a
truth-loving man, then will I affirm that those same initials denote
Envenomed Wickedness!"</p>
<hr style="width: 45%;">
<p class="center">CLASS LIST.</p>
<p><span style="margin-left: 12.5em;">I.</span></p>
<p>
<span style="margin-left: 10.5em;"><span class="smcap">A Marlborough Boy.</span></span><br>
<span style="margin-left: 10.5em;"><span class="smcap">Putney Walker.</span></span>

<p><span style="margin-left: 12.5em;">II.</span></p>
<p>
<span style="margin-left: 10.5em;"><span class="smcap">Blithe.</span></span><br>
<span style="margin-left: 10.5em;">E. W.</span><br>
<span style="margin-left: 10.5em;">L. B.</span><br>
<span style="margin-left: 10.5em;">O. V. L.</span><br>
<span style="margin-left: 10.5em;"><span class="smcap">Rose.</span></span><br>
<span style="margin-left: 10.5em;"><span class="smcap">Sea Breeze.</span></span><br>
<span style="margin-left: 10.5em;">{<span class="smcap">Simple Susan.</span></span><br>
<span style="margin-left: 10.5em;">{<span class="smcap">Money-Spinner.</span></span><br>
<span class="pagenum"><a id="Page_82">[82]</a></span></p>
<p><span class="smcap">Blithe</span> has made so ingenious an addition to the problem, and <span class="smcap">Simple
Susan</span> and <span class="smcap">Co</span>. have solved it in such tuneful verse, that I record both
their answers in full. I have altered a word or two in <span class="smcap">Blithe's</span>—which I
trust she will excuse; it did not seem quite clear as it stood.</p>
<hr style="width: 45%;">
<p>"Yet stay," said the youth, as a gleam of inspiration lighted up the
relaxing muscles of his quiescent features. "Stay. Methinks it matters
little <i>when</i> we reached that summit, the crown of our toil. For in the
space of time wherein we clambered up one mile and bounded down the same
on our return, we could have trudged the <i>twain</i> on the level. We have
plodded, then, four-and-twenty miles in these six mortal hours; for
never a moment did we stop for catching of fleeting breath or for gazing
on the scene around!"</p>
<p>"Very good," said the old man. "Twelve miles out and twelve miles in.
And we reached the top some time between six and seven of the clock. Now
mark me! For every five minutes that had fled since six of the clock
when we stood on yonder peak, so many miles had we toiled upwards on the
dreary mountainside!"</p>
<p>The youth moaned and rushed into the hostel.</p>
<p class="author"><span class="smcap">Blithe.</span></p>
<hr style="width: 45%;">

<h3>ANSWERS TO KNOT II.</h3>
<p class="fm3">§ 1. <span class="smcap">The Dinner Party.</span></p>
<p><i>Problem.</i>—"The Governor of Kgovjni wants to give a very small dinner
party, and invites his father's brother-in-law, his brother's
father-in-law, his father-in-law's brother, and his brother-in-law's
father. Find the number of guests."</p>
<p><i>Answer.</i>—"One."</p>
<hr style="width: 45%;">
<p>In this genealogy, males are denoted by capitals, and females by small
letters.</p>
<p>The Governor is E and his guest is C.</p>
<div class="figright" style="width: 400px;">
<img alt="" height="243" src="images/i097.png" title="" width="400" id="img_images_i097.png">
</div>
<p>Ten answers have been received. Of these, one is wrong, <span class="smcap">Galanthus
Nivalis Major</span>, who insists on inviting <i>two</i> guests, one being the
Governor's <i>wife's brother's father</i>. If she had taken his <i>sister's
husband's father</i> instead, she would have found it possible to reduce
the guests to <i>one</i>.<span class="pagenum"><a id="Page_85">[85]</a></span></p>
<p>Of the nine who send right answers, <span class="smcap">Sea-Breeze</span> is the very faintest
breath that ever bore the name! She simply states that the Governor's
uncle might fulfill all the conditions "by intermarriages"! "Wind of the
western sea," you have had a very narrow escape! Be thankful to appear
in the Class-list at all! <span class="smcap">Bog-Oak</span> and <span class="smcap">Bradshaw of the Future</span> use
genealogies which require 16 people instead of 14, by inviting the
Governor's <i>father's sister's husband</i> instead of his <i>father's wife's
brother</i>. I cannot think this so good a solution as one that requires
only 14. <span class="smcap">Caius</span> and <span class="smcap">Valentine</span> deserve special mention as the only two who
have supplied genealogies.</p>
<p class="center">CLASS LIST.</p>
<p><span style="margin-left: 12.5em;">I.</span></p>
<p>
<span style="margin-left: 10.5em;"><span class="smcap">Bee.</span></span><br>
<span style="margin-left: 10.5em;"><span class="smcap">Caius.</span></span><br>
<span style="margin-left: 10.5em;">M. M.</span><br>
<span style="margin-left: 10.5em;"><span class="smcap">Matthew Matticks.</span></span><br>
<span style="margin-left: 10.5em;"><span class="smcap">Old Cat.</span></span><br>
<span style="margin-left: 10.5em;"><span class="smcap">Valentine.</span></span><br>
</p>
<p><span style="margin-left: 12.5em;">II.</span></p>
<p>
<span style="margin-left: 10.5em;"><span class="smcap">Bog-Oak.</span></span><br>
<span style="margin-left: 10.5em;"><span class="smcap">Bradshaw of the Future.</span></span><br>
</p>
<p><span style="margin-left: 12.5em;">III.</span></p>
<p>
<span style="margin-left: 10.5em;"><span class="smcap">Sea-Breeze.</span></span><br>
<span class="pagenum"><a id="Page_86">[86]</a></span></p>
<p class="fm3">§ 2. <span class="smcap">The Lodgings.</span></p>
<p><i>Problem.</i>—"A Square has 20 doors on each side, which contains 21 equal
parts. They are numbered all round, beginning at one corner. From which
of the four, Nos. 9, 25, 52, 73, is the sum of the distances, to the
other three, least?"</p>
<p><i>Answer.</i>—"From No. 9."</p>
<hr style="width: 45%;">
<div class="figright" style="width: 319px;">
<img alt="" height="372" src="images/i099.png" title="" width="319" id="img_images_i099.png">
</div>
<p>Let A be No. 9, B No. 25, C No. 52, and D No. 73.</p>
<p>
<span style="margin-left: 1.5em;">Then AB = √(12<sup>2</sup> + 5<sup>2</sup>) = √169 = 13;</span><br>
<span style="margin-left: 1.5em;">AC = 21;</span><br>
<span style="margin-left: 1.5em;">AD = √(9<sup>2</sup> + 8<sup>2</sup>) = √145 = 12+</span><br>
<span style="margin-left: 1.5em;">(N.B. <i>i.e.</i> "between 12 and 13.")</span><br>
<span style="margin-left: 1.5em;">BC = √(16<sup>2</sup> + 12<sup>2</sup>) = √400 = 20;</span><br>
<span style="margin-left: 1.5em;">BD = √(3<sup>2</sup> + 21<sup>2</sup>) = √450 = 21+;</span><br>
<span style="margin-left: 1.5em;">CD = √(9<sup>2</sup> + 13<sup>2</sup>) = √250 = 15+;</span><br>
</p>
<p>Hence sum of distances from A is between 46 and 47; from B, between 54
and 55; from C, between 56 and 57; from D, between 48 and 51. (Why not
"between 48 and 49"? Make this out for yourselves.) Hence the sum is
least for A.</p>
<hr style="width: 45%;">
<p><span class="pagenum"><a id="Page_87">[87]</a></span></p>
<p>Twenty-five solutions have been received. Of these, 15 must be marked
"0," 5 are partly right, and 5 right. Of the 15, I may dismiss
<span class="smcap">Alphabetical Phantom</span>, <span class="smcap">Bog-Oak</span>, <span class="smcap">Dinah Mite</span>, <span class="smcap">Fifee</span>, <span class="smcap">Galanthus Nivalis
Major</span> (I fear the cold spring has blighted our <span class="smcap">Snowdrop</span>), <span class="smcap">Guy</span>, <span class="smcap">H.M.S.
Pinafore</span>, <span class="smcap">Janet</span>, and <span class="smcap">Valentine</span> with the simple remark that they insist
on the unfortunate lodgers <i>keeping to the pavement</i>. (I used the words
"crossed to Number Seventy-three" for the special purpose of showing
that <i>short cuts</i> were possible.) <span class="smcap">Sea-Breeze</span> does the same, and adds
that "the result would be the same" even if they crossed the Square, but
gives no proof of this. M. M. draws a diagram, and says that No. 9 is
the house, "as the diagram shows." I cannot see <i>how</i> it does so. <span class="smcap">Old
Cat</span> assumes that the house <i>must</i> be No. 9 or No. 73. She does not
explain how she estimates the distances. BEE's Arithmetic is faulty: she
makes √169 + √442 + √130 = 741. (I suppose you
mean √741, which would be a little nearer the truth. But roots
cannot be added in this manner. Do you think √9 + √16 is
25, or even √25?) But <span class="smcap">Ayr's</span> state is more perilous still: she
draws illogical conclusions with a frightful calmness. After pointing
out (rightly) that AC is less than BD she says, "therefore the nearest
house to the other three must be A or C." And again, after pointing out
(rightly) that B and D are both within the half-square containing<span class="pagenum"><a id="Page_88">[88]</a></span> A,
she says "therefore" AB + AD must be less than BC + CD. (There is no
logical force in either "therefore." For the first, try Nos. 1, 21, 60,
70: this will make your premiss true, and your conclusion false.
Similarly, for the second, try Nos. 1, 30, 51, 71.)</p>
<p>Of the five partly-right solutions, <span class="smcap">Rags and Tatters</span> and <span class="smcap">Mad Hatter</span> (who
send one answer between them) make No. 25 6 units from the corner
instead of 5. <span class="smcap">Cheam</span>, E. R. D. L., and <span class="smcap">Meggy Potts</span> leave openings at
<a id="corr1"></a><a class="correction pginternal" href="#cn1" title="changed from 'he'">the</a>
corners of the Square, which are not in the <i>data</i>: moreover <span class="smcap">Cheam</span> gives
values for the distances without any hint that they are only
<i>approximations</i>. <span class="smcap">Crophi and Mophi</span> make the bold and unfounded
assumption that there were really 21 houses on each side, instead of 20
as stated by Balbus. "We may assume," they add, "that the doors of Nos.
21, 42, 63, 84, are invisible from the centre of the Square"! What is
there, I wonder, that <span class="smcap">Crophi and Mophi</span> would <i>not</i> assume?</p>
<p>Of the five who are wholly right, I think <span class="smcap">Bradshaw Of the Future</span>, <span class="smcap">Caius</span>,
<span class="smcap">Clifton C.</span>, and <span class="smcap">Martreb</span> deserve special praise for their full
<i>analytical</i> solutions. <span class="smcap">Matthew Matticks</span> picks out No. 9, and proves it
to be the right house in two ways, very neatly and ingeniously, but
<i>why</i> he picks it out does not appear. It is an excellent <i>synthetical</i>
proof, but lacks the analysis which the other four supply.</p>
<p><span class="pagenum"><a id="Page_89">[89]</a></span></p>
<p class="center">CLASS LIST.</p>
<p><span style="margin-left: 12.5em;">I.</span></p>
<p>
<span style="margin-left: 10.5em;"><span class="smcap">Bradshaw of the Future</span></span><br>
<span style="margin-left: 10.5em;"><span class="smcap">Caius.</span></span><br>

<p><span style="margin-left: 12.5em;">III.</span></p>
<p>
<span style="margin-left: 10.5em;"><span class="smcap">Cheam.</span></span><br>
<span style="margin-left: 10.5em;"><span class="smcap">Crophi and Mophi.</span></span><br>
<span style="margin-left: 10.5em;"><span class="smcap">E. R. D. L.</span></span><br>
<span style="margin-left: 10.5em;"><span class="smcap">Meggy Potts.</span></span><br>
<span style="margin-left: 10.5em;">{<span class="smcap">Rags and Tatters.</span></span><br>
<span style="margin-left: 10.5em;">{<span class="smcap">Mad Hatter.</span></span><br>
</p>
<p>A remonstrance has reached me from <span class="smcap">Scrutator</span> on the subject of <span class="smcap">Knot I.</span>,
which he declares was "no problem at all." "Two questions," he says,
"are put. To solve one there is no data: the other answers itself." As
to the first point, <span class="smcap">Scrutator</span> is mistaken; there <i>are</i> (not "is") data
sufficient to answer the question. As to the other, it is interesting to
know that the question "answers itself," and I am sure it does the
question great credit: still I fear I cannot enter it on the list of
winners, as this competition is only open to human beings.</p>
<hr style="width: 45%;">
<p><span class="pagenum"><a id="Page_90">[90]</a></span></p>
<h3>ANSWERS TO KNOT III.</h3>
<p><i>Problem.</i>—(1) "Two travellers, starting at the same time, went
opposite ways round a circular railway. Trains start each way every 15
minutes, the easterly ones going round in 3 hours, the westerly in 2.
How many trains did each meet on the way, not counting trains met at the
terminus itself?" (2) "They went round, as before, each traveller
counting as 'one' the train containing the other traveller. How many did
each meet?"</p>
<p><i>Answers.</i>—(1) 19. (2) The easterly traveller met 12; the other 8.</p>
<hr style="width: 45%;">
<p>The trains one way took 180 minutes, the other way 120. Let us take the
L. C. M., 360, and divide the railway into 360 units. Then one set of
trains went at the rate of 2 units a minute and at intervals of 30
units; the other at the rate of 3 units a minute and at intervals of 45
units. An easterly train starting has 45 units between it and the first
train it will meet: it does 2-5ths of this while the other does 3-5ths,
and<span class="pagenum"><a id="Page_91">[91]</a></span> thus meets it at the end of 18 units, and so all the way round. A
westerly train starting has 30 units between it and the first train it
will meet: it does 3-5ths of this while the other does 2-5ths, and thus
meets it at the end of 18 units, and so all the way round. Hence if the
railway be divided, by 19 posts, into 20 parts, each containing 18
units, trains meet at every post, and, in (1), each traveller passes 19
posts in going round, and so meets 19 trains. But, in (2), the easterly
traveller only begins to count after traversing 2-5ths of the journey,
<i>i.e.</i>, on reaching the 8th post, and so counts 12 posts: similarly the
other counts 8. They meet at the end of 2-5ths of 3 hours, or 3-5ths of
2 hours, <i>i.e.</i>, 72 minutes.</p>
<hr style="width: 45%;">
<p>Forty-five answers have been received. Of these 12 are beyond the reach
of discussion, as they give no working. I can but enumerate their names.
<span class="smcap">Ardmore</span>, E. A., F. A. D., L. D., <span class="smcap">Matthew Matticks</span>, M. E. T., <span class="smcap">Poo-Poo</span>,
and <span class="smcap">The Red Queen</span> are all wrong. <span class="smcap">Beta</span> and <span class="smcap">Rowena</span> have got (1) right and
(2) wrong. <span class="smcap">Cheeky Bob</span> and <span class="smcap">Nairam</span> give the right answers, but it may
perhaps make the one less cheeky, and induce the other to take a less
inverted view of things, to be informed that, if this had been a
competition for a<span class="pagenum"><a id="Page_92">[92]</a></span> prize, they would have got no marks. [N.B.—I have
not ventured to put E. A.'s name in full, as she only gave it
provisionally, in case her answer should prove right.]</p>
<p>Of the 33 answers for which the working is given, 10 are wrong; 11
half-wrong and half-right; 3 right, except that they cherish the
delusion that it was <i>Clara</i> who travelled in the easterly train—a
point which the data do not enable us to settle; and 9 wholly right.</p>
<p>The 10 wrong answers are from <span class="smcap">Bo-Peep</span>, <span class="smcap">Financier</span>, I. W. T., <span class="smcap">Kate B.</span>, M.
A. H., Q. Y. Z., <span class="smcap">Sea-Gull</span>, <span class="smcap">Thistledown</span>, <span class="smcap">Tom-Quad</span>, and an unsigned one.
<span class="smcap">Bo-Peep</span> rightly says that the easterly traveller met all trains which
started during the 3 hours of her trip, as well as all which started
during the previous 2 hours, <i>i.e.</i>, all which started at the
commencements of 20 periods of 15 minutes each; and she is right in
striking out the one she met at the moment of starting; but wrong in
striking out the <i>last</i> train, for she did not meet this at the
terminus, but 15 minutes before she got there. She makes the same
mistake in (2). <span class="smcap">Financier</span> thinks that any train, met for the second
time, is not to be counted. I. W. T. finds, by a process which is not
stated, that the travellers met at the end of 71 minutes and 26½
seconds. <span class="smcap">Kate B.</span> thinks the trains which are met on starting and on
arriving<span class="pagenum"><a id="Page_93">[93]</a></span> are <i>never</i> to be counted, even when met elsewhere. Q. Y. Z.
tries a rather complex algebraical solution, and succeeds in finding the
time of meeting correctly: all else is wrong. <span class="smcap">Sea-Gull</span> seems to think
that, in (1), the easterly train <i>stood still</i> for 3 hours; and says
that, in (2), the travellers met at the end of 71 minutes 40 seconds.
<span class="smcap">Thistledown</span> nobly confesses to having tried no calculation, but merely
having drawn a picture of the railway and counted the trains; in (1),
she counts wrong; in (2) she makes them meet in 75 minutes. <span class="smcap">Tom-Quad</span>
omits (1): in (2) he makes Clara count the train she met on her arrival.
The unsigned one is also unintelligible; it states that the travellers
go "1-24th more than the total distance to be traversed"! The "Clara"
theory, already referred to, is adopted by 5 of these, viz., <span class="smcap">Bo-Peep</span>,
<span class="smcap">Financier</span>, <span class="smcap">Kate B.</span>, <span class="smcap">Tom-Quad</span>, and the nameless writer.</p>
<p>The 11 half-right answers are from <span class="smcap">Bog-Oak</span>, <span class="smcap">Bridget</span>, <span class="smcap">Castor</span>, <span class="smcap">Cheshire
Cat</span>, G. E. B., <span class="smcap">Guy</span>, <span class="smcap">Mary</span>, M. A. H., <span class="smcap">Old Maid</span>, R. W., and <span class="smcap">Vendredi</span>. All
these adopt the "Clara" theory. <span class="smcap">Castor</span> omits (1). <span class="smcap">Vendredi</span> gets (1)
right, but in (2) makes the same mistake as <span class="smcap">Bo-Peep</span>. I notice in your
solution a marvellous proportion-sum:—"300 miles: 2 hours :: one mile:
24 seconds." May I venture to advise your acquiring, as soon as
possible, an utter disbelief in the possibility of a ratio<span class="pagenum"><a id="Page_94">[94]</a></span> existing
between <i>miles</i> and <i>hours</i>? Do not be disheartened by your two friends'
sarcastic remarks on your "roundabout ways." Their short method, of
adding 12 and 8, has the slight disadvantage of bringing the answer
wrong: even a "roundabout" method is better than <i>that</i>! M. A. H., in
(2), makes the travellers count "one" <i>after</i> they met, not <i>when</i> they
met. <span class="smcap">Cheshire Cat</span> and <span class="smcap">Old Maid</span> get "20" as answer for (1), by forgetting
to strike out the train met on arrival. The others all get "18" in
various ways. <span class="smcap">Bog-Oak</span>, <span class="smcap">Guy</span>, and R. W. divide the trains which the
westerly traveller has to meet into 2 sets, viz., those already on the
line, which they (rightly) make "11," and those which started during her
2 hours' journey (exclusive of train met on arrival), which they
(wrongly) make "7"; and they make a similar mistake with the easterly
train. <span class="smcap">Bridget</span> (rightly) says that the westerly traveller met a train
every 6 minutes for 2 hours, but (wrongly) makes the number "20"; it
should be "21." G. E. B. adopts <span class="smcap">Bo-Peep's</span> method, but (wrongly) strikes
out (for the easterly traveller) the train which started at the
<i>commencement</i> of the previous 2 hours. <span class="smcap">Mary</span> thinks a train, met on
arrival, must not be counted, even when met on a <i>previous</i> occasion.</p>
<p>The 3, who are wholly right but for the unfortunate "Clara" theory, are
<span class="smcap">F. Lee</span>, G. S. C., and X. A. B.</p>
<p>And now "descend, ye classic Ten!" who have<span class="pagenum"><a id="Page_95">[95]</a></span> solved the whole problem.
Your names are
<span class="smcap">Aix-les-Bains</span>,
<span class="smcap">Algernon Bray</span> (thanks for a friendly
remark, which comes with a heart-warmth that not even the Atlantic could
chill), <span class="smcap">Arvon</span>, <span class="smcap">Bradshaw of the Future</span>, <span class="smcap">Fifee</span>, H. L. R., J. L. O., <span class="smcap">Omega</span>,
S. S. G., and <span class="smcap">Waiting for the Train</span>. Several of these have put Clara,
provisionally, into the easterly train: but they seem to have understood
that the data do not decide that point.</p>
<p class="center">CLASS LIST.</p>

<p><span class="pagenum"><a id="Page_96">[96]</a></span></p>
<h3>ANSWERS TO KNOT IV.</h3>
<p><i>Problem.</i>—"There are 5 sacks, of which Nos. 1, 2, weigh 12 lbs.; Nos.
2, 3, 13½ lbs.; Nos. 3, 4, 11½ lbs.; Nos. 4, 5, 8 lbs.; Nos. 1, 3,
5, 16 lbs. Required the weight of each sack."</p>
<p><i>Answer.</i>—"5½, 6½, 7, 4½, 3½."</p>
<hr style="width: 45%;">
<p>The sum of all the weighings, 61 lbs., includes sack No. 3 <i>thrice</i> and
each other <i>twice</i>. Deducting twice the sum of the 1st and 4th
weighings, we get 21 lbs. for <i>thrice</i> No. 3, <i>i.e.</i>, 7 lbs. for No. 3.
Hence, the 2nd and 3rd weighings give 6½ lbs., 4½ lbs. for Nos. 2,
4; and hence again, the 1st and 4th weighings give 5½ lbs., 3½
lbs., for Nos. 1, 5.</p>
<hr style="width: 45%;">
<p>Ninety-seven answers have been received. Of these, 15 are beyond the
reach of discussion, as they give no working. I can but enumerate their
names, and I take this opportunity of saying that this is the last time
I shall put on record the names of competitors who give no<span class="pagenum"><a id="Page_97">[97]</a></span> sort of clue
to the process by which their answers were obtained. In guessing a
conundrum, or in catching a flea, we do not expect the breathless victor
to give us afterwards, in cold blood, a history of the mental or
muscular efforts by which he achieved success; but a mathematical
calculation is another thing. The names of this "mute inglorious" band
are <span class="smcap">Common Sense</span>, D. E. R., <span class="smcap">Douglas</span>, E. L., <span class="smcap">Ellen</span>, I. M. T., J. M. C.,
<span class="smcap">Joseph</span>, <span class="smcap">Knot I</span>, <span class="smcap">Lucy</span>, <span class="smcap">Meek</span>, M. F. C., <span class="smcap">Pyramus</span>, <span class="smcap">Shah</span>, <span class="smcap">Veritas</span>.</p>
<p>Of the eighty-two answers with which the working, or some approach to
it, is supplied, one is wrong: seventeen have given solutions which are
(from one cause or another) practically valueless: the remaining
sixty-four I shall try to arrange in a Class-list, according to the
varying degrees of shortness and neatness to which they seem to have
attained.</p>
<p>The solitary wrong answer is from <span class="smcap">Nell</span>. To be thus "alone in the crowd"
is a distinction—a painful one, no doubt, but still a distinction. I am
sorry for you, my dear young lady, and I seem to hear your tearful
exclamation, when you read these lines, "Ah! This is the knell of all my
hopes!" Why, oh why, did you assume that the 4th and 5th bags weighed 4
lbs. each? And why did you not test your answers? However, please try
again: and please don't change your <i>nom-de-plume</i>: let us have <span class="smcap">Nell</span> in
the First Class next time!<span class="pagenum"><a id="Page_98">[98]</a></span></p>
<p>The seventeen whose solutions are practically valueless are <span class="smcap">Ardmore</span>, <span class="smcap">A
ready Reckoner</span>, <span class="smcap">Arthur</span>, <span class="smcap">Bog-Lark</span>, <span class="smcap">Bog-Oak</span>, <span class="smcap">Bridget</span>, <span class="smcap">First Attempt</span>, J. L.
C., M. E. T., <span class="smcap">Rose</span>, <span class="smcap">Rowena</span>, <span class="smcap">Sea-Breeze</span>, <span class="smcap">Sylvia</span>, <span class="smcap">Thistledown</span>,
<span class="smcap">Three-Fifths Asleep</span>, <span class="smcap">Vendredi</span>, and <span class="smcap">Winifred</span>. <span class="smcap">Bog-Lark</span> tries it by a sort
of "rule of false," assuming experimentally that Nos. 1, 2, weigh 6 lbs.
each, and having thus produced 17½, instead of 16, as the weight of
1, 3, and 5, she removes "the superfluous pound and a half," but does
not explain how she knows from which to take it. <span class="smcap">Three-fifths Asleep</span>
says that (when in that peculiar state) "it seemed perfectly clear" to
her that, "3 out of the 5 sacks being weighed twice over, <sup>2</sup>⁄<sub>5</sub> of 45 =
27, must be the total weight of the 5 sacks." As to which I can only
say, with the Captain, "it beats me entirely!" <span class="smcap">Winifred</span>, on the plea
that "one must have a starting-point," assumes (what I fear is a mere
guess) that No. 1 weighed 5½ lbs. The rest all do it, wholly or
partly, by guess-work.</p>
<p>The problem is of course (as any Algebraist sees at once) a case of
"simultaneous simple equations." It is, however, easily soluble by
Arithmetic only; and, when this is the case, I hold that it is bad
workmanship to use the more complex method. I have not, this time, given
more credit to arithmetical solutions; but in future problems I shall
(other things being equal) give the<span class="pagenum"><a id="Page_99">[99]</a></span> highest marks to those who use the
simplest machinery. I have put into Class I. those whose answers seemed
specially short and neat, and into Class III. those that seemed
specially long or clumsy. Of this last set, A. C. M., <span class="smcap">Furze-Bush</span>, <span class="smcap">James</span>,
<span class="smcap">Partridge</span>, R. W., and <span class="smcap">Waiting for the Train</span>, have sent long wandering
solutions, the substitutions having no definite method, but seeming to
have been made to see what would come of it. <span class="smcap">Chilpome</span> and <span class="smcap">Dublin Boy</span>
omit some of the working. <span class="smcap">Arvon Marlborough Boy</span> only finds the weight of
<i>one</i> sack.<span class="pagenum"><a id="Page_100">[100]</a></span></p>

<h3>ANSWERS TO KNOT V.</h3>

to 9 or 10; also giving 3 o's to 1 or 2, 2 to 3 or 4 and 1 to 8 or 9; so

<p>By then assigning o's in the same way, beginning at the other end, we
get 9 pictures marked thus:—</p>

<p>All we have now to do is to run these two wedges<span class="pagenum"><a id="Page_103">[103]</a></span> as close together as
they will go, so as to get the minimum number of pictures——erasing
optional marks where by so doing we can run them closer, but otherwise
letting them stand. There are 10 necessary marks in the 1st row, and in
the 3rd; but only 7 in the 2nd. Hence we erase all optional marks in the
1st and 3rd rows, but let them stand in the 2nd.</p>
<hr style="width: 45%;">
<p>Twenty-two answers have been received. Of these 11 give no working; so,
in accordance with what I announced in my last review of answers, I
leave them unnamed, merely mentioning that 5 are right and 6 wrong.</p>
<p>Of the eleven answers with which some working is supplied, 3 are wrong.
C. H. begins with the rash assertion that under the given conditions
"the sum is impossible. For," he or she adds (these initialed
correspondents are dismally vague beings to deal with: perhaps "it"
would be a better pronoun), "10 is the least possible number of
pictures" (granted): "therefore we must either give 2 x's to 6, or 2 o's
to 5." Why "must," oh alphabetical phantom? It is nowhere ordained that
every picture "must" have 3 marks! <span class="smcap">Fifee</span> sends a folio page of solution,
which deserved a better fate: she offers 3 answers, in each of which 10
pictures are<span class="pagenum"><a id="Page_104">[104]</a></span> marked, with 30 marks; in one she gives 2 x's to 6
pictures; in another to 7; in the 3rd she gives 2 o's to 5; thus in
every case ignoring the conditions. (I pause to remark that the
condition "2 x's to 4 or 5 pictures" can only mean "<i>either</i> to 4 <i>or
else</i> to 5": if, as one competitor holds, it might mean <i>any</i> number not
less than 4, the words "<i>or</i> 5" would be superfluous.) I. E. A. (I am
happy to say that none of these bloodless phantoms appear this time in
the class-list. Is it IDEA with the "D" left out?) gives 2 x's to 6
pictures. She then takes me to task for using the word "ought" instead
of "nought." No doubt, to one who thus rebels against the rules laid
down for her guidance, the word must be distasteful. But does not I. E.
A. remember the parallel case of "adder"? That creature was originally
"a nadder": then the two words took to bandying the poor "n" backwards
and forwards like a shuttlecock, the final state of the game being "an
adder." May not "a nought" have similarly become "an ought"? Anyhow,
"oughts and crosses" is a very old game. I don't think I ever heard it
called "noughts and crosses."</p>
<p>In the following Class-list, I hope the solitary occupant of III. will
sheathe her claws when she hears how narrow an escape she has had of not
being named at all. Her account of the process by which she got the
answer is so meagre that, like the nursery tale of "Jack-a-Minory" (I<span class="pagenum"><a id="Page_105">[105]</a></span>
trust I. E. A. will be merciful to the spelling), it is scarcely to be
distinguished from "zero."</p>

<hr style="width: 45%;">
<p><span class="pagenum"><a id="Page_106">[106]</a></span></p>
<h3>ANSWERS TO KNOT VI.</h3>
<p><i>Problem 1.</i>—<i>A</i> and <i>B</i> began the year with only 1,000<i>l.</i> a-piece.
They borrowed nought; they stole nought. On the next New-Year's Day they
had 60,000<i>l.</i> between them. How did they do it?</p>
<p><i>Solution.</i>—They went that day to the Bank of England. <i>A</i> stood in
front of it, while <i>B</i> went round and stood behind it.</p>
<hr style="width: 45%;">
<p>Two answers have been received, both worthy of much honour. <span class="smcap">Addlepate</span>
makes them borrow "0" and steal "0," and uses both cyphers by putting
them at the right-hand end of the 1,000<i>l.</i>, thus producing 100,000<i>l.</i>,
which is well over the mark. But (or to express it in Latin) <span class="smcap">At Spes
infracta</span> has solved it even more ingeniously: with the first cypher she
turns the "1" of the 1,000<i>l.</i> into a "9," and adds the result to the
original sum, thus getting 10,000<i>l.</i>: and in this, by means of the
other "0," she turns the "1" into a "6," thus hitting the exact
60,000<i>l.</i><span class="pagenum"><a id="Page_107">[107]</a></span></p>
<p class="center">CLASS LIST</p>
<p><span style="margin-left: 12.5em;">I.</span></p>
<p><span style="margin-left: 10.5em;"><span class="smcap">At Spes Infracta.</span></span></p>
<p><span style="margin-left: 12.5em;">II.</span></p>
<p><span style="margin-left: 10.5em;"><span class="smcap">Addlepate.</span></span></p>
<hr style="width: 45%;">
<p><i>Problem 2.</i>—<i>L</i> makes 5 scarves, while <i>M</i> makes 2: <i>Z</i> makes 4 while
<i>L</i> makes 3. Five scarves of <i>Z</i>'s weigh one of <i>L</i>'s; 5 of <i>M</i>'s weigh
3 of <i>Z</i>'s. One of <i>M</i>'s is as warm as 4 of <i>Z</i>'s: and one of <i>L</i>'s as
warm as 3 of <i>M</i>'s. Which is best, giving equal weight in the result to
rapidity of work, lightness, and warmth?</p>
<p><i>Answer.</i>—The order is <i>M</i>, <i>L</i>, <i>Z</i>.</p>
<hr style="width: 45%;">
<p><i>Solution.</i>—As to rapidity (other things being constant) <i>L</i>'s merit is
to <i>M</i>'s in the ratio of 5 to 2: <i>Z</i>'s to <i>L</i>'s in the ratio of 4 to 3.
In order to get one set of 3 numbers fulfilling these conditions, it is
perhaps simplest to take the one that occurs <i>twice</i> as unity, and
reduce the others to fractions: this gives, for <i>L</i>, <i>M</i>, and <i>Z</i>, the
marks 1, <sup>2</sup>⁄<sub>5</sub>, <sup>2</sup>⁄<sub>3</sub>. In estimating for <i>lightness</i>, we observe that the
greater the weight, the less the merit, so that <i>Z</i>'s merit is to <i>L</i>'s
as 5 to 1. Thus the marks for <i>lightness</i> are <sup>1</sup>⁄<sub>5</sub>, <sup>2</sup>⁄<sub>3</sub>, 1. And
similarly, the marks for warmth are 3, 1, ¼. To get the<span class="pagenum"><a id="Page_108">[108]</a></span> total result,
we must <i>multiply</i> <i>L</i>'s 3 marks together, and do the same for <i>M</i> and
for <i>Z</i>. The final numbers are 1 × <sup>1</sup>⁄<sub>5</sub> × 3, <sup>2</sup>⁄<sub>5</sub> × <sup>2</sup>⁄<sub>3</sub> × 1,
<sup>2</sup>⁄<sub>3</sub> × 1 ×
¼; <i>i.e.</i> <sup>3</sup>⁄<sub>5</sub>,
<a id="corr3"></a><a class="correction pginternal" href="#cn3" title="changed from '2'"><sup>2</sup>⁄<sub>3</sub></a>, <sup>1</sup>⁄<sub>3</sub>; <i>i.e.</i> multiplying throughout by 15 (which
will not alter the proportion), 9, 10, 5; showing the order of merit to
be <i>M</i>, <i>L</i>, <i>Z</i>.</p>
<hr style="width: 45%;">
<p>Twenty-nine answers have been received, of which five are right, and
twenty-four wrong. These hapless ones have all (with three exceptions)
fallen into the error of <i>adding</i> the proportional numbers together, for
each candidate, instead of <i>multiplying</i>. <i>Why</i> the latter is right,
rather than the former, is fully proved in text-books, so I will not
occupy space by stating it here: but it can be <i>illustrated</i> very easily
by the case of length, breadth, and depth. Suppose <i>A</i> and <i>B</i> are rival
diggers of rectangular tanks: the amount of work done is evidently
measured by the number of <i>cubical feet</i> dug out. Let <i>A</i> dig a tank 10
feet long, 10 wide, 2 deep: let <i>B</i> dig one 6 feet long, 5 wide, 10
deep. The cubical contents are 200, 300; <i>i.e.</i> <i>B</i> is best digger in
the ratio of 3 to 2. Now try marking for length, width, and depth,
separately; giving a maximum mark of 10 to the best in each contest, and
then <i>adding</i> the results!</p>
<p>Of the twenty-four malefactors, one gives no working, and so has no real
claim to be named; but I break the rule for once, in deference to its
success in Problem 1:<span class="pagenum"><a id="Page_109">[109]</a></span> he, she, or it, is <span class="smcap">Addlepate</span>. The other
twenty-three may be divided into five groups.</p>
<p>First and worst are, I take it, those who put the rightful winner
<i>last</i>; arranging them as "Lolo, Zuzu, Mimi." The names of these
desperate wrong-doers are <span class="smcap">Ayr</span>, <span class="smcap">Bradshaw of the Future</span>, <span class="smcap">Furze-bush</span> and
<span class="smcap">Pollux</span> (who send a joint answer), <span class="smcap">Greystead</span>, <span class="smcap">Guy</span>, <span class="smcap">Old Hen</span>, and <span class="smcap">Simple
Susan</span>. The latter was <i>once</i> best of all; the Old Hen has taken
advantage of her simplicity, and beguiled her with the chaff which was
the bane of her own chickenhood.</p>
<p>Secondly, I point the finger of scorn at those who have put the worst
candidate at the top; arranging them as "Zuzu, Mimi, Lolo." They are
<span class="smcap">Graecia</span>, M. M., <span class="smcap">Old Cat</span>, and R. E. X. "'Tis Greece, but——."</p>
<p>The third set have avoided both these enormities, and have even
succeeded in putting the worst last, their answer being "Lolo, Mimi,
Zuzu." Their names are <span class="smcap">Ayr</span> (who also appears among the "quite too too"),
<span class="smcap">Clifton C.</span>, F. B., <span class="smcap">Fifee</span>, <span class="smcap">Grig</span>, <span class="smcap">Janet</span>, and <span class="smcap">Mrs. Sairey Gamp</span>. F. B. has
not fallen into the common error; she <i>multiplies</i> together the
proportionate numbers she gets, but in getting them she goes wrong, by
reckoning warmth as a <i>de</i>-merit. Possibly she is "Freshly Burnt," or
comes "From Bombay." <span class="smcap">Janet</span> and <span class="smcap">Mrs. Sairey Gamp</span> have also avoided this
error: the method they have adopted is<span class="pagenum"><a id="Page_110">[110]</a></span> shrouded in mystery—I scarcely
feel competent to criticize it. <span class="smcap">Mrs. Gamp</span> says "if Zuzu makes 4 while
Lolo makes 3, Zuzu makes 6 while Lolo makes 5 (bad reasoning), while
Mimi makes 2." From this she concludes "therefore Zuzu excels in speed
by 1" (<i>i.e.</i> when compared with Lolo; but what about Mimi?). She then
compares the 3 kinds of excellence, measured on this mystic scale. <span class="smcap">Janet</span>
takes the statement, that "Lolo makes 5 while Mimi makes 2," to prove
that "Lolo makes 3 while Mimi makes 1 and Zuzu 4" (worse reasoning than
<span class="smcap">Mrs. Gamp's</span>), and thence concludes that "Zuzu excels in speed by <sup>1</sup>⁄<sub>8</sub>"!
<span class="smcap">Janet</span> should have been <span class="smcap">Adeline</span>, "mystery of mysteries!"</p>
<p>The fourth set actually put Mimi at the top, arranging them as "Mimi,
Zuzu, Lolo." They are <span class="smcap">Marquis and Co.</span>, <span class="smcap">Martreb</span>, S. B. B. (first initial
scarcely legible: <i>may</i> be meant for "J"), and <span class="smcap">Stanza</span>.</p>
<p>The fifth set consist of <span class="smcap">An ancient Fish</span> and <span class="smcap">Camel</span>. These ill-assorted
comrades, by dint of foot and fin, have scrambled into the right answer,
but, as their method is wrong, of course it counts for nothing. Also <span class="smcap">An
ancient Fish</span> has very ancient and fishlike ideas as to <i>how</i> numbers
represent merit: she says "Lolo gains 2½ on Mimi." Two and a half
<i>what</i>? Fish, fish, art thou in thy duty?</p>
<p>Of the five winners I put <span class="smcap">Balbus</span> and <span class="smcap">The elder Traveller</span> slightly below
the other three—<span class="smcap">Balbus</span> for<span class="pagenum"><a id="Page_111">[111]</a></span> defective reasoning, the other for scanty
working. <span class="smcap">Balbus</span> gives two reasons for saying that <i>addition</i> of marks is
<i>not</i> the right method, and then adds "it follows that the decision must
be made by <i>multiplying</i> the marks together." This is hardly more
logical than to say "This is not Spring: <i>therefore</i> it must be Autumn."</p>
<p class="center">CLASS LIST.</p>
<p><span style="margin-left: 12.5em;">I.</span></p>
<p>
<span style="margin-left: 10.5em;"><span class="smcap">Dinah Mite.</span></span><br>
<span style="margin-left: 10.5em;">E. B. D. L.</span><br>
<span style="margin-left: 10.5em;"><span class="smcap">Joram.</span></span><br>
</p>
<p><span style="margin-left: 12.5em;">II.</span></p>
<p>
<span style="margin-left: 10.5em;"><span class="smcap">Balbus.</span></span><br>
<span style="margin-left: 10.5em;"><span class="smcap">The Elder Traveller.</span></span><br>
</p>
<hr style="width: 45%;">
<p>With regard to Knot V., I beg to express to <span class="smcap">Vis Inertiæ</span> and to any
others who, like her, understood the condition to be that <i>every</i> marked
picture must have <i>three</i> marks, my sincere regret that the unfortunate
phrase "<i>fill</i> the columns with oughts and crosses" should have caused
them to waste so much time and trouble. I can only repeat that a
<i>literal</i> interpretation of "fill" would seem to <i>me</i> to require that
<i>every</i> picture in the gallery should be marked. <span class="smcap">Vis Inertiæ</span> would have
been in the First Class if she had sent in the solution she now offers.</p>
<hr style="width: 45%;">
<p><span class="pagenum"><a id="Page_112">[112]</a></span></p>
<h3>ANSWERS TO KNOT VII.</h3>
<p><i>Problem.</i>—Given that one glass of lemonade, 3 sandwiches, and 7
biscuits, cost 1<i>s.</i> 2<i>d.</i>; and that one glass of lemonade, 4
sandwiches, and 10 biscuits, cost 1<i>s.</i> 5<i>d.</i>: find the cost of (1) a
glass of lemonade, a sandwich, and a biscuit; and (2) 2 glasses of
lemonade, 3 sandwiches, and 5 biscuits.</p>
<p><i>Answer.</i>—(1) 8<i>d.</i>; (2) 1<i>s.</i> 7<i>d.</i></p>
<p><i>Solution.</i>—This is best treated algebraically. Let <i>x</i> = the cost (in
pence) of a glass of lemonade, <i>y</i> of a sandwich, and <i>z</i> of a biscuit.
Then we have <i>x</i> + 3<i>y</i> + 7<i>z</i> = 14, and <i>x</i> + 4<i>y</i> + 10<i>z</i> = 17. And we
require the values of <i>x</i> + <i>y</i> + <i>z</i>, and of 2<i>x</i> + 3<i>y</i> + 5<i>z</i>. Now,
from <i>two</i> equations only, we cannot find, <i>separately</i>, the values of
<i>three</i> unknowns: certain <i>combinations</i> of them may, however, be found.
Also we know that we can, by the help of the given equations, eliminate
2 of the 3 unknowns from the quantity whose value is required, which
will then contain one only. If, then, the required value is
ascertainable at all, it can only be by the 3rd unknown vanishing of
itself: otherwise the problem is impossible.<span class="pagenum"><a id="Page_113">[113]</a></span></p>
<p>Let us then eliminate lemonade and sandwiches, and reduce everything to
biscuits—a state of things even more depressing than "if all the world
were apple-pie"—by subtracting the 1st equation from the 2nd, which
eliminates lemonade, and gives <i>y</i> + 3<i>z</i> = 3, or <i>y</i> = 3-3<i>z</i>; and then
substituting this value of <i>y</i> in the 1st, which gives <i>x</i>-2<i>z</i> = 5,
<i>i.e.</i> <i>x</i> = 5 + 2<i>z</i>. Now if we substitute these values of <i>x</i>, <i>y</i>, in
the quantities whose values are required, the first becomes (5 + 2<i>z</i>) +
(3-3<i>z</i>) + <i>z</i>, <i>i.e.</i> 8: and the second becomes 2(5 + 2<i>z</i>) + 3(3-3<i>z</i>)
+ 5<i>z</i>, <i>i.e.</i> 19. Hence the answers are (1) 8<i>d.</i>, (2) 1<i>s.</i> 7<i>d.</i></p>
<hr style="width: 45%;">
<p>The above is a <i>universal</i> method: that is, it is absolutely certain
either to produce the answer, or to prove that no answer is possible.
The question may also be solved by combining the quantities whose values
are given, so as to form those whose values are required. This is merely
a matter of ingenuity and good luck: and as it <i>may</i> fail, even when the
thing is possible, and is of no use in proving it <i>im</i>possible, I cannot
rank this method as equal in value with the other. Even when it
succeeds, it may prove a very tedious process. Suppose the 26
competitors, who have sent in what I may call <i>accidental</i> solutions,
had had a question to deal with where every number contained 8 or 10
digits! I suspect it would have been a case of "silvered is the raven
hair" (see<span class="pagenum"><a id="Page_114">[114]</a></span> "Patience") before any solution would have been hit on by
the most ingenious of them.</p>
<p>Forty-five answers have come in, of which 44 give, I am happy to say,
some sort of <i>working</i>, and therefore deserve to be mentioned by name,
and to have their virtues, or vices as the case may be, discussed.
Thirteen have made assumptions to which they have no right, and so
cannot figure in the Class-list, even though, in 10 of the
<a id="corr4"></a><a class="correction pginternal" href="#cn4" title="changed from '12'">13</a> cases, the
answer is right. Of the remaining 28, no less than 26 have sent in
<i>accidental</i> solutions, and therefore fall short of the highest honours.</p>
<p>I will now discuss individual cases, taking the worst first, as my
custom is.</p>
<p><span class="smcap">Froggy</span> gives no working—at least this is all he gives: after stating
the given equations, he says "therefore the difference, 1 sandwich + 3
biscuits, = 3<i>d.</i>": then follow the amounts of the unknown bills, with
no further hint as to how he got them. <span class="smcap">Froggy</span> has had a <i>very</i> narrow
escape of not being named at all!</p>
<p>Of those who are wrong, <span class="smcap">Vis Inertiæ</span> has sent in a piece of incorrect
working. Peruse the horrid details, and shudder! She takes <i>x</i> (call it
"<i>y</i>") as the cost of a sandwich, and concludes (rightly enough) that a
biscuit will cost (3-<i>y</i>)/3. She then subtracts the second equation from
the first, and deduces 3<i>y</i> + 7 × (3-<i>y</i>)/3-4<i>y</i> + 10 × (3-<i>y</i>)/3 = 3.<span class="pagenum"><a id="Page_115">[115]</a></span>
By making two mistakes in this line, she brings out <i>y</i> = <sup>2</sup>⁄<sub>2</sub>. Try it
again, oh <span class="smcap">Vis Inertiæ</span>! Away with <span class="smcap">Inertiæ</span>: infuse a little more <span class="smcap">Vis</span>: and
you will bring out the correct (though uninteresting) result, 0 = 0!
This will show you that it is hopeless to try to coax any one of these 3
unknowns to reveal its <i>separate</i> value. The other competitor, who is
wrong throughout, is either J. M. C. or T. M. C.: but, whether he be a
Juvenile Mis-Calculator or a True Mathematician Confused, he makes the
answers 7<i>d.</i> and 1<i>s.</i> 5<i>d.</i> He assumes, with Too Much Confidence, that
biscuits were ½<i>d.</i> each, and that Clara paid for 8, though she only
ate 7!</p>
<p>We will now consider the 13 whose working is wrong, though the answer is
right: and, not to measure their demerits too exactly, I will take them
in alphabetical order. <span class="smcap">Anita</span> finds (rightly) that "1 sandwich and 3
biscuits cost 3<i>d.</i>," and proceeds "therefore 1 sandwich = 1½<i>d.</i>, 3
biscuits = 1½<i>d.</i>, 1 lemonade = 6<i>d.</i>" <span class="smcap">Dinah Mite</span> begins like <span class="smcap">Anita</span>:
and thence proves (rightly) that a biscuit costs less than a 1<i>d.</i>:
whence she concludes (wrongly) that it <i>must</i> cost ½<i>d.</i> F. C. W. is
so beautifully resigned to the certainty of a verdict of "guilty," that
I have hardly the heart to utter the word, without adding a "recommended
to mercy owing to extenuating circumstances." But really, you know,
where <i>are</i> the extenuating<span class="pagenum"><a id="Page_116">[116]</a></span> circumstances? She begins by assuming that
lemonade is 4<i>d.</i> a glass, and sandwiches 3<i>d.</i> each, (making with the 2
given equations, <i>four</i> conditions to be fulfilled by <i>three</i> miserable
unknowns!). And, having (naturally) developed this into a contradiction,
she then tries 5<i>d.</i> and 2<i>d.</i> with a similar result. (N.B. <i>This</i>
process might have been carried on through the whole of the Tertiary
Period, without gratifying one single Megatherium.) She then, by a
"happy thought," tries half-penny biscuits, and so obtains a consistent
result. This may be a good solution, viewing the problem as a conundrum:
but it is <i>not</i> scientific. <span class="smcap">Janet</span> identifies sandwiches with biscuits!
"One sandwich + 3 biscuits" she makes equal to "4." Four <i>what</i>? <span class="smcap">Mayfair</span>
makes the astounding assertion that the equation, <i>s</i> + 3<i>b</i> = 3, "is
evidently only satisfied by <i>s</i> = <sup>2</sup>⁄<sub>2</sub>, <i>b</i> = ½"! <span class="smcap">Old Cat</span> believes that
the assumption that a sandwich costs 1½<i>d.</i> is "the only way to avoid
unmanageable fractions." But <i>why</i> avoid them? Is there not a certain
glow of triumph in taming such a fraction? "Ladies and gentlemen, the
fraction now before you is one that for years defied all efforts of a
refining nature: it was, in a word, hopelessly vulgar. Treating it as a
circulating decimal (the treadmill of fractions) only made matters
worse. As a last resource, I reduced it to its lowest terms, and
extracted its square root!" Joking<span class="pagenum"><a id="Page_117">[117]</a></span> apart, let me thank <span class="smcap">Old Cat</span> for some
very kind words of sympathy, in reference to a correspondent (whose name
I am happy to say I have now forgotten) who had found fault with me as a
discourteous critic. O. V. L. is beyond my comprehension. He takes the
given equations as (1) and (2): thence, by the process [(2)-(1)] deduces
(rightly) equation (3) viz. <i>s</i> + 3<i>b</i> = 3: and thence again, by the
process [×33] (a hopeless mystery), deduces 3<i>s</i> + 4<i>b</i> = 4. I have
nothing to say about it: I give it up. <span class="smcap">Sea-Breeze</span> says "it is immaterial
to the answer" (why?) "in what proportion 3<i>d.</i> is divided between the
sandwich and the 3 biscuits": so she assumes <i>s</i> = l½<i>d.</i>, <i>b</i> =
½<i>d.</i> <span class="smcap">Stanza</span> is one of a very irregular metre. At first she (like
<span class="smcap">Janet</span>) identifies sandwiches with biscuits. She then tries two
assumptions (<i>s</i> = 1, <i>b</i> = <sup>2</sup>⁄<sub>3</sub>, and <i>s</i> = ½ <i>b</i> = <sup>2</sup>⁄<sub>6</sub>), and
(naturally) ends in contradictions. Then she returns to the first
assumption, and finds the 3 unknowns separately: <i>quod est absurdum</i>.
<span class="smcap">Stiletto</span> identifies sandwiches and biscuits, as "articles." Is the word
ever used by confectioners? I fancied "What is the next article, Ma'am?"
was limited to linendrapers. <span class="smcap">Two Sisters</span> first assume that biscuits are
4 a penny, and then that they are 2 a penny, adding that "the answer
will of course be the same in both cases." It is a dreamy<span class="pagenum"><a id="Page_118">[118]</a></span> remark,
making one feel something like Macbeth grasping at the spectral dagger.
"Is this a statement that I see before me?" If you were to say "we both
walked the same way this morning," and <i>I</i> were to say "<i>one</i> of you
walked the same way, but the other didn't," which of the three would be
the most hopelessly confused? <span class="smcap">Turtle Pyate</span> (what <i>is</i> a Turtle Pyate,
please?) and <span class="smcap">Old Crow</span>, who send a joint answer, and Y. Y., adopt the
same method. Y. Y. gets the equation <i>s</i> + 3<i>b</i> = 3: and then says "this
sum must be apportioned in one of the three following ways." It <i>may</i>
be, I grant you: but Y. Y. do you say "must"? I fear it is <i>possible</i>
for Y. Y. to be <i>two</i> Y's. The other two conspirators are less positive:
they say it "can" be so divided: but they add "either of the three
prices being right"! This is bad grammar and bad arithmetic at once, oh
mysterious birds!</p>
<p>Of those who win honours, <span class="smcap">The Shetland Snark</span> must have the 3rd class all
to himself. He has only answered half the question, viz. the amount of
Clara's luncheon: the two little old ladies he pitilessly leaves in the
midst of their "difficulty." I beg to assure him (with thanks for his
friendly remarks) that entrance-fees and subscriptions are things
unknown in that most economical of clubs, "The Knot-Untiers."</p>
<p>The authors of the 26 "accidental" solutions differ only in the number
of steps they have taken between the<span class="pagenum"><a id="Page_119">[119]</a></span> <i>data</i> and the answers. In order
to do them full justice I have arranged the 2nd class in sections,
according to the number of steps. The two Kings are fearfully
deliberate! I suppose walking quick, or taking short cuts, is
inconsistent with kingly dignity: but really, in reading <span class="smcap">Theseus'</span>
solution, one almost fancied he was "marking time," and making no
advance at all! The other King will, I hope, pardon me for having
altered "Coal" into "Cole." King Coilus, or Coil, seems to have reigned
soon after Arthur's time. Henry of Huntingdon identifies him with the
King Coël who first built walls round Colchester, which was named after
him. In the Chronicle of Robert of Gloucester we read:—</p>
<div class="poem"><div class="stanza">
<span class="i0">"Aftur Kyng Aruirag, of wam we habbeth y told,<br></span>
<span class="i0">Marius ys sone was kyng, quoynte mon &amp; bold.<br></span>
<span class="i0">And ys sone was aftur hym, <i>Coil</i> was ys name,<br></span>
<span class="i0">Bothe it were quoynte men, &amp; of noble fame."<br></span>
</div></div>
<p><span class="smcap">Balbus</span> lays it down as a general principle that "in order to ascertain
the cost of any one luncheon, it must come to the same amount upon two
different assumptions." (<i>Query.</i> Should not "it" be "we"? Otherwise the
<i>luncheon</i> is represented as wishing to ascertain its own cost!) He then
makes two assumptions—one, that sandwiches cost nothing; the other,
that biscuits cost nothing, (either arrangement would lead to the shop
being inconveniently crowded!)—and brings out the unknown<span class="pagenum"><a id="Page_120">[120]</a></span> luncheons as
8<i>d.</i> and 19<i>d.</i>, on each assumption. He then concludes that this
agreement of results "shows that the answers are correct." Now I propose
to disprove his general law by simply giving <i>one</i> instance of its
failing. One instance is quite enough. In logical language, in order to
disprove a "universal affirmative," it is enough to prove its
contradictory, which is a "particular negative." (I must pause for a
digression on Logic, and especially on Ladies' Logic. The universal
affirmative "everybody says he's a duck" is crushed instantly by proving
the particular negative "Peter says he's a goose," which is equivalent
to "Peter does <i>not</i> say he's a duck." And the universal negative
"nobody calls on her" is well met by the particular affirmative "<i>I</i>
called yesterday." In short, either of two contradictories disproves the
other: and the moral is that, since a particular proposition is much
more easily proved than a universal one, it is the wisest course, in
arguing with a Lady, to limit one's <i>own</i> assertions to "particulars,"
and leave <i>her</i> to prove the "universal" contradictory, if she can. You
will thus generally secure a <i>logical</i> victory: a <i>practical</i> victory is
not to be hoped for, since she can always fall back upon the crushing
remark "<i>that</i> has nothing to do with it!"—a move for which Man has not
yet discovered any satisfactory answer. Now let us return to <span class="smcap">Balbus</span>.)
Here is my "particular negative," on which to test his rule. Suppose the
two<span class="pagenum"><a id="Page_121">[121]</a></span> recorded luncheons to have been "2 buns, one queen-cake, 2
sausage-rolls, and a bottle of Zoëdone: total, one-and-ninepence," and
"one bun, 2 queen-cakes, a sausage-roll, and a bottle of Zoëdone: total,
one-and-fourpence." And suppose Clara's unknown luncheon to have been "3
buns, one queen-cake, one sausage-roll, and 2 bottles of Zoëdone:" while
the two little sisters had been indulging in "8 buns, 4 queen-cakes, 2
sausage-rolls, and 6 bottles of Zoëdone." (Poor souls, how thirsty they
must have been!) If <span class="smcap">Balbus</span> will kindly try this by his principle of "two
assumptions," first assuming that a bun is 1<i>d.</i> and a queen-cake 2<i>d.</i>,
and then that a bun is 3<i>d.</i> and a queen-cake 3<i>d.</i>, he will bring out
the other two luncheons, on each assumption, as "one-and-nine-pence" and
"four-and-ten-pence" respectively, which harmony of results, he will
say, "shows that the answers are correct." And yet, as a matter of fact,
the buns were 2<i>d.</i> each, the queen-cakes 3<i>d.</i>, the sausage-rolls
6<i>d.</i>, and the Zoëdone 2<i>d.</i> a bottle: so that Clara's third luncheon
had cost one-and-sevenpence, and her thirsty friends had spent
<a id="corr5"></a><a class="correction pginternal" href="#cn5" title="changed from 'four-and fourpence'">four-and-fourpence</a>!</p>
<p>Another remark of <span class="smcap">Balbus</span> I will quote and discuss: for I think that it
also may yield a moral for some of my readers. He says "it is the same
thing in substance whether in solving this problem we use words and call
it Arithmetic, or use letters and signs and call it Algebra."<span class="pagenum"><a id="Page_122">[122]</a></span> Now this
does not appear to me a correct description of the two methods: the
Arithmetical method is that of "synthesis" only; it goes from one known
fact to another, till it reaches its goal: whereas the Algebraical
method is that of "analysis": it begins with the goal, symbolically
represented, and so goes backwards, dragging its veiled victim with it,
till it has reached the full daylight of known facts, in which it can
tear off the veil and say "I know you!"</p>
<p>Take an illustration. Your house has been broken into and robbed, and
you appeal to the policeman who was on duty that night. "Well, Mum, I
did see a chap getting out over your garden-wall: but I was a good bit
off, so I didn't chase him, like. I just cut down the short way to the
Chequers, and who should I meet but Bill Sykes, coming full split round
the corner. So I just ups and says 'My lad, you're wanted.' That's all I
says. And he says 'I'll go along quiet, Bobby,' he says, 'without the
darbies,' he says." There's your <i>Arithmetical</i> policeman. Now try the
other method. "I seed somebody a running, but he was well gone or ever
<i>I</i> got nigh the place. So I just took a look round in the garden. And I
noticed the foot-marks, where the chap had come right across your
flower-beds. They was good big foot-marks sure-ly. And I noticed as the
left foot went down at the heel, ever so much deeper than the other. And
I says to myself<span class="pagenum"><a id="Page_123">[123]</a></span> 'The chap's been a big hulking chap: and he goes lame
on his left foot.' And I rubs my hand on the wall where he got over, and
there was soot on it, and no mistake. So I says to myself 'Now where can
I light on a big man, in the chimbley-sweep line, what's lame of one
foot?' And I flashes up permiscuous: and I says 'It's Bill Sykes!' says
I." There is your <i>Algebraical</i> policeman—a higher intellectual type,
to my thinking, than the other.</p>
<p><span class="smcap">Little Jack's</span> solution calls for a word of praise, as he has written out
what really is an algebraical proof <i>in words</i>, without representing any
of his facts as equations. If it is all his own, he will make a good
algebraist in the time to come. I beg to thank <span class="smcap">Simple Susan</span> for some
kind words of sympathy, to the same effect as those received from <span class="smcap">Old
Cat</span>.</p>
<p><span class="smcap">Hecla</span> and <span class="smcap">Martreb</span> are the only two who have used a method <i>certain</i>
either to produce the answer, or else to prove it impossible: so they
must share between them the highest honours.<span class="pagenum"><a id="Page_124">[124]</a></span></p>

<p><span class="pagenum"><a id="Page_125">[125]</a></span></p>
<h3>ANSWERS TO CORRESPONDENTS.</h3>
<p>I have received several letters on the subjects of Knots II. and VI.,
which lead me to think some further explanation desirable.</p>
<p>In Knot II., I had intended the numbering of the houses to begin at one
corner of the Square, and this was assumed by most, if not all, of the
competitors. <span class="smcap">Trojanus</span> however says "assuming, in default of any
information, that the street enters the square in the middle of each
side, it may be supposed that the numbering begins at a street." But
surely the other is the more natural assumption?</p>
<p>In Knot VI., the first Problem was of course a mere <i>jeu de mots</i>, whose
presence I thought excusable in a series of Problems whose aim is to
entertain rather than to instruct: but it has not escaped the
contemptuous criticisms of two of my correspondents, who seem to think
that Apollo is in duty bound to keep his bow always on the stretch.
Neither of them has guessed it: and this is true human nature. Only the
other day—the 31st of September, to be quite exact—I met my old friend
Brown, and gave him a riddle I had just heard. With one great effort of
his colossal mind, Brown guessed it. "Right!" said I. "Ah," said<span class="pagenum"><a id="Page_126">[126]</a></span> he,
"it's very neat—very neat. And it isn't an answer that would occur to
everybody. Very neat indeed." A few yards further on, I fell in with
Smith and to him I propounded the same riddle. He frowned over it for a
minute, and then gave it up. Meekly I faltered out the answer. "A poor
thing, sir!" Smith growled, as he turned away. "A very poor thing! I
wonder you care to repeat such rubbish!" Yet Smith's mind is, if
possible, even more colossal than Brown's.</p>
<p>The second Problem of Knot VI. is an example in ordinary Double Rule of
Three, whose essential feature is that the result depends on the
variation of several elements, which are so related to it that, if all
but one be constant, it varies as that one: hence, if none be constant,
it varies as their product. Thus, for example, the cubical contents of a
rectangular tank vary as its length, if breadth and depth be constant,
and so on; hence, if none be constant, it varies as the product of the
length, breadth, and depth.</p>
<p>When the result is not thus connected with the varying elements, the
Problem ceases to be Double Rule of Three and often becomes one of great
complexity.</p>
<p>To illustrate this, let us take two candidates for a prize, <i>A</i> and <i>B</i>,
who are to compete in French, German, and Italian:</p>
<p>(<i>a</i>) Let it be laid down that the result is to depend<span class="pagenum"><a id="Page_127">[127]</a></span> on their
<i>relative</i> knowledge of each subject, so that, whether their marks, for
French, be "1, 2" or "100, 200," the result will be the same: and let it
also be laid down that, if they get equal marks on 2 papers, the final
marks are to have the same ratio as those of the 3rd paper. This is a
case of ordinary Double Rule of Three. We multiply <i>A</i>'s 3 marks
together, and do the same for <i>B</i>. Note that, if <i>A</i> gets a single "0,"
his final mark is "0," even if he gets full marks for 2 papers while <i>B</i>
gets only one mark for each paper. This of course would be very unfair
on <i>A</i>, though a correct solution under the given conditions.</p>
<p>(<i>b</i>) The result is to depend, as before, on <i>relative</i> knowledge; but
French is to have twice as much weight as German or Italian. This is an
unusual form of question. I should be inclined to say "the resulting
ratio is to be nearer to the French ratio than if we multiplied as in
(<i>a</i>), and so much nearer that it would be necessary to use the other
multipliers <i>twice</i> to produce the same result as in (<i>a</i>):" <i>e.g.</i> if
the French Ratio were <sup>2</sup>⁄<sub>10</sub>, and the others <sup>2</sup>⁄<sub>9</sub>, <sup>1</sup>⁄<sub>9</sub> so that the ultimate
ratio, by method (<i>a</i>), would be <sup>2</sup>⁄<sub>45</sub>, I should multiply instead by <sup>2</sup>⁄<sub>3</sub>,
<sup>1</sup>⁄<sub>3</sub>, giving the result, <sup>1</sup>⁄<sub>3</sub> which is nearer to <sup>2</sup>⁄<sub>10</sub> than if he had used
method (<i>a</i>).</p>
<p>(<i>c</i>) The result is to depend on <i>actual</i> amount of knowledge of the 3
subjects collectively. Here we have<span class="pagenum"><a id="Page_128">[128]</a></span> to ask two questions. (1) What is
to be the "unit" (<i>i.e.</i> "standard to measure by") in each subject? (2)
Are these units to be of equal, or unequal value? The usual "unit" is
the knowledge shown by answering the whole paper correctly; calling this
"100," all lower amounts are represented by numbers between "0" and
"100." Then, if these units are to be of equal value, we simply add
<i>A</i>'s 3 marks together, and do the same for <i>B</i>.</p>
<p>(<i>d</i>) The conditions are the same as (<i>c</i>), but French is to have double
weight. Here we simply double the French marks, and add as before.</p>
<p>(<i>e</i>) French is to have such weight, that, if other marks be equal, the
ultimate ratio is to be that of the French paper, so that a "0" in this
would swamp the candidate: but the other two subjects are only to affect
the result collectively, by the amount of knowledge shown, the two being
reckoned of equal value. Here I should add <i>A</i>'s German and Italian
marks together, and multiply by his French mark.</p>
<p>But I need not go on: the problem may evidently be set with many varying
conditions, each requiring its own method of solution. The Problem in
Knot VI. was meant to belong to variety (<i>a</i>), and to make this clear, I
inserted the following passage:</p>
<p>"Usually the competitors differ in one point only. Thus, last year, Fifi
and Gogo made the same number of<span class="pagenum"><a id="Page_129">[129]</a></span> scarves in the trial week, and they
were equally light; but Fifi's were twice as warm as Gogo's, and she was
pronounced twice as good."</p>
<p>What I have said will suffice, I hope, as an answer to <span class="smcap">Balbus</span>, who holds
that (<i>a</i>) and (<i>c</i>) are the only possible varieties of the problem, and
that to say "We cannot use addition, therefore we must be intended to
use multiplication," is "no more illogical than, from knowledge that one
was not born in the night, to infer that he was born in the daytime";
and also to <span class="smcap">Fifee</span>, who says "I think a little more consideration will
show you that our 'error of <i>adding</i> the proportional numbers together
for each candidate instead of <i>multiplying</i>' is no error at all." Why,
even if addition <i>had</i> been the right method to use, not one of the
writers (I speak from memory) showed any consciousness of the necessity
of fixing a "unit" for each subject. "No error at all!" They were
positively steeped in error!</p>
<p>One correspondent (I do not name him, as the communication is not quite
friendly in tone) writes thus:—"I wish to add, very respectfully, that
I think it would be in better taste if you were to abstain from the very
trenchant expressions which you are accustomed to indulge in when
criticising the answer. That such a tone must not be" ("be not"?)
"agreeable to<span class="pagenum"><a id="Page_130">[130]</a></span> the persons concerned who have made mistakes may possibly
have no great weight with you, but I hope you will feel that it would be
as well not to employ it, <i>unless you are quite certain of being correct
yourself</i>." The only instances the writer gives of the "trenchant
expressions" are "hapless" and "malefactors." I beg to assure him (and
any others who may need the assurance: I trust there are none) that all
such words have been used in jest, and with no idea that they could
possibly annoy any one, and that I sincerely regret any annoyance I may
have thus inadvertently given. May I hope that in future they will
recognise the distinction between severe language used in sober earnest,
and the "words of unmeant bitterness," which Coleridge has alluded to in
that lovely passage beginning "A little child, a limber elf"? If the
writer will refer to that passage, or to the preface to "Fire, Famine,
and Slaughter," he will find the distinction, for which I plead, far
better drawn out than I could hope to do in any words of mine.</p>
<p>The writer's insinuation that I care not how much annoyance I give to my
readers I think it best to pass over in silence; but to his concluding
remark I must entirely demur. I hold that to use language likely to
annoy any of my correspondents would not be in the least justified by
the plea that I was "quite certain of<span class="pagenum"><a id="Page_131">[131]</a></span> being correct." I trust that the
knot-untiers and I are not on such terms as those!</p>
<p>I beg to thank <i>G. B.</i> for the offer of a puzzle—which, however, is too
like the old one "Make four 9's into 100."</p>
<hr style="width: 45%;">
<p><span class="pagenum"><a id="Page_132">[132]</a></span></p>

<p class="fm3">§ 1. <span class="smcap">The Pigs.</span></p>
